🔁 Where to Return After an Error — Rav Huna vs. Rav Asi on whether the middle blessings are one unit
🙇 Servant Before the Master — praise, request, and leave-taking; who bows where, and the three kinds of bowing
⏱️ Too Long, Too Short — Rabbi Eliezer defends both from Moses; no need to name the sick

overview.title: 📖 Overview: The Prayer Leader and the Power of Prayer
overview.subtitle: Berakhot 34a–34b
overview.hebrewSource: אִם שְׁגוּרָה תְּפִלָּתִי בְּפִי — יוֹדֵעַ אֲנִי שֶׁהוּא מְקוּבָּל, וְאִם לָאו — יוֹדֵעַ אֲנִי שֶׁהוּא מְטוֹרָף
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: Two mishnayot on the communal prayer leader close the chapter. The first: a leader who errs is replaced at once, the replacement may not refuse, and he resumes from the blessing where the error occurred — which sends the Gemara into the etiquette of refusing the honor, the structure of the Amida's three sections, and the choreography of bowing. Rabbi Eliezer defends a student who prayed too long and another who prayed too short, both from Moses. The second mishna: an error in prayer is a bad omen, and Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa could tell from the fluency of his prayer whether a sick person would live. The Gemara ends with what 'no eye has seen' — the reward stored for those who support Torah scholars, for the World-to-Come, and for the fully righteous — and with Rav Kahana's two impudences.

slides.title: 🧂 How to Accept the Honor of Leading Prayer
slides.subtitle: The baraita's three-step etiquette, and why refusal is like salt

steps.content: 1️⃣ Mishna: if the leader errs, another passes before the ark in his place and must not refuse at that moment; he begins from the start of the blessing in which the first erred
2️⃣ Baraita: ordinarily one asked to lead should refuse — one who jumps at it is like a dish without salt; one who refuses too much is like a dish ruined by salt
3️⃣ First request — refuse; second — waver like a wick just catching flame (מְהַבְהֵב); third — stretch out his legs and descend
4️⃣ Three things are harmful in excess and good in moderation: leaven, salt, and refusal (שְׂאוֹר, וּמֶלַח, וְסָרְבָנוּת)

callout.label: Guarding against confusion:
callout.text: The leader does not answer amen after the priests' blessing, lest he lose his place. If he is the only priest present he does not lift his hands — unless he is confident he can bless and return to his prayer without confusion.

slides.title: 🔁 Three Sections, Three Postures — and Where to Go Back
slides.subtitle: Rav Huna, Rav Asi, Rav Yehuda and Rabbi Ḥanina map the Amida
rows: A servant arranging praise before his master
No — Rav Yehuda: never in the first three
A servant requesting a reward from his master
A servant who received his reward and takes leave
No — never in the last three

callout.label: Rav Asi vs. Rav Huna:
callout.text: Rav Asi: the middle blessings have no fixed order — one inserts the missed blessing wherever he realizes. Rav Sheshet objected from the baraita 'he begins from the start of the blessing in which he erred' — a refutation of Rav Huna? Rav Huna answers: the middle blessings are all one blessing, so 'its start' is Ata Ḥonen.

slides.title: 🙇 Who Bows, Where, and How
slides.subtitle: A Tosefta on the fixed bows, two versions of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, and a baraita on the vocabulary of bowing

boxes.title: Ordinary person
items: Bows at the beginning and end of Patriarchs (Avot)
Bows at the beginning and end of Thanksgiving (Hoda'ah)
One who wants to bow at every blessing is taught not to

boxes.title: High Priest and King
items: Bar Kappara's version: the High Priest bows at the end of every blessing; the king at the beginning and end of every blessing

Rabbi Yitzḥak bar Naḥmani heard from Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: the High Priest at the beginning of each; the king, once he bows, does not rise — Solomon 'rose from kneeling on his knees' only when he finished (I Kings 8:54)
The loftier the status, the more submission is shown

boxes.title: Three words for bowing
items: Kidda — on the face: 'Bathsheba bowed with her face to the ground' (I Kings 1:31)
Keria — on the knees: Solomon 'from kneeling upon his knees'
Hishtaḥava'a — hands and legs spread: 'shall we come and bow down to you to the ground?' (Genesis 37:10)
Rav Ḥiyya son of Rav Huna: Abaye and Rava merely leaned

callout.label: Rava bowed in Thanksgiving, beginning and end:
callout.text: The Sages asked why. 'I saw Rav Naḥman and Rav Sheshet do so.' But a baraita calls bowing in Thanksgiving reprehensible! — That is bowing at its end (or in the Thanksgiving of Hallel). But another baraita says 'in Thanksgiving and in the Thanksgiving of Hallel'! — That refers to the Thanksgiving blessing of Grace after Meals.

slides.title: ⏱️ Too Long, Too Short — Rabbi Eliezer Answers His Students
slides.subtitle: Two incidents before the ark, and a rule about praying for the sick

lines.speaker: Students
lines.text: A student led the prayer before Rabbi Eliezer and went on and on. 'How long-winded he is!'

lines.speaker: R' Eliezer
lines.text: Is he longer than Moses our teacher? 'I prostrated myself before the Lord for the forty days and forty nights' (Deut. 9:25).

lines.speaker: Students
lines.text: Another student led before Rabbi Eliezer and was over in a moment. 'How brief he is!'

lines.speaker: R' Eliezer
lines.text: Is he briefer than Moses our teacher? אֵל נָא רְפָא נָא לָהּ — 'Please, God, heal her, please' (Numbers 12:13).

lines.speaker: Rav Ḥisda
lines.text: And from that same verse, Rabbi Ya'akov reports: one who asks mercy for another need not mention his name — Moses did not name Miriam.

callout.label: Takeaway:
callout.text: There is no fixed length for prayer; both the forty-day prayer and the five-word prayer are Moses' own.

slides.title: 🩺 Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa: 'This One Will Live, This One Will Die'
slides.subtitle: The final mishna on errors as omens, and the source of Rabbi Ḥanina's confidence

nodes.content: 📜 Mishna: one who errs in his prayer — a bad omen for him; a prayer leader who errs — a bad omen for those who sent him, for a person's agent is like himself
❓ In which blessing? Rav Safra in the name of Rabbi's school: in Avot. (Some apply this to the baraita: if one cannot focus in all the blessings, focus at least in one — Avot)
🗣️ Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa prayed for the sick and announced who would live and who would die: 'If my prayer is fluent in my mouth, I know it is accepted; if not, I know it is rejected'
📖 Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's source: 'He who creates the expression of the lips… peace, peace to the far and the near, says the Lord — and I will heal him' (Isaiah 57:19)

columns.label: Rabban Gamliel's son
columns.content: Two scholars sent to Rabbi Ḥanina; he went up to the attic, prayed, came down: 'Go — the fever has left him.' 'Are you a prophet?' 'Neither a prophet nor a prophet's son, but this is my tradition.' They wrote down the hour; Rabban Gamliel: 'By the Temple service — at that very moment the fever broke and he asked for water.'

columns.label: R' Yoḥanan ben Zakkai's son
columns.content: Rabbi Ḥanina put his head between his knees, prayed, and the boy lived. 'Had ben Zakkai done so all day, they would not have heeded him.' His wife: 'Is Ḥanina greater than you?' 'No — he is like a servant before the king, and I like a minister before the king.'

callout.label: 'No eye has seen' (Isaiah 64:3):
callout.text: Rabbi Yoḥanan: the prophets foretold reward only for one who marries his daughter to a scholar, does business for him, or supports him — for scholars themselves, 'no eye has seen'; only the days of the Messiah — for the World-to-Come, 'no eye has seen'; only penitents — for the fully righteous, 'no eye has seen'. Shmuel disagrees: the only difference in the Messiah's days is freedom from foreign rule. Rabbi Abbahu disagrees: where penitents stand the fully righteous cannot — 'peace to the far' comes first. What is it? Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: wine kept in its grapes since Creation; Rabbi Shmuel bar Naḥmani: Eden itself — not the Garden, for 'a river went out from Eden to water the Garden.'

summary.principle: The Amida is a servant's audience with the King — praise, request, leave — and the one who leads it must carry both its etiquette and its weight: the fluency of the words themselves testifies whether the prayer was received.

flowSteps.content: 🧂 Asked to lead: refuse, waver, then go — refusal is like salt, good only in small measure
🔁 Error in the first three → beginning; in the middle → Ata Ḥonen (Rav Huna) or wherever he recalls (Rav Asi); in the last three → Avoda
🙇 Bow in Avot and Hoda'ah, beginning and end; High Priest and king bow more; kidda, keria, hishtaḥava'a

columns.content: ⏱️ Long like Moses' forty days or short like 'El na refa na lah' — both valid
🩺 Fluent prayer = accepted prayer; Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa, servant before the King

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: Pray in a house with windows, not in a field, and do not spell out your sins — 'happy is he whose transgression is covered' (Rav Kahana)

quiz.q: According to the baraita, how should one respond when asked to serve as prayer leader?
o: Accept immediately, so as not to burden the congregation
Refuse the first time, waver the second, and go up the third
Refuse three times before accepting
Accept only if no priest is present
quiz.e: One who does not refuse at all is like a dish without salt; one who refuses too much is like a dish ruined by salt. So: refuse once, vacillate 'like a wick catching flame' the second time, and descend before the ark the third.

quiz.q: What is the dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Asi about an error in the middle blessings of the Amida?
o: Rav Huna: return to the beginning of the Amida; Rav Asi: return to Avoda
Rav Huna: return to 'You grace humanity', since the middle blessings are one unit; Rav Asi: they have no fixed order, so insert the missed blessing wherever one realizes
Rav Huna: repeat the whole Amida; Rav Asi: do nothing
They dispute only the last three blessings
quiz.e: Rav Huna treats the thirteen middle blessings as a single blessing, so one returns to its start, Ata Ḥonen — which is how he answers Rav Sheshet's objection from the baraita. Rav Asi holds the middle blessings have no fixed order.

quiz.q: How did Rabbi Eliezer defend the student whose prayer was excessively brief?
o: He said brevity is always preferable in public prayer
He cited Moses' five-word prayer for Miriam, 'Please, God, heal her, please'
He said the student had already prayed privately
He cited Hannah, whose voice was not heard
quiz.e: Just as he defended the long-winded student from Moses' forty days and nights of prostration, Rabbi Eliezer defended the brief one from Moses' prayer in Numbers 12:13 — no one is briefer than that.

quiz.q: How did Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa know whether a sick person would recover?
o: He was a prophet, as he told Rabban Gamliel's messengers
By examining the patient in person
If his prayer was fluent in his mouth he knew it was accepted; if not, he knew it was rejected
By whether the fever broke while he was still praying
quiz.e: He explicitly denied being a prophet or a prophet's son; his received tradition was that fluency of the prayer signals acceptance, which Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi grounds in Isaiah 57:19, 'He who creates the expression of the lips… and I will heal him.'

quiz.q: How did Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Zakkai explain why Rabbi Ḥanina ben Dosa's prayer for his son succeeded when his own would not?
o: Rabbi Ḥanina was the greater scholar
Rabbi Ḥanina is like a servant before the king, who may enter at any time, while he is like a minister, who enters only when summoned
Rabbi Ḥanina prayed in a house with windows
Rabbi Ḥanina's prayer was longer
quiz.e: When his wife asked whether Ḥanina was greater than he, Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Zakkai said no — but a servant has constant, informal access to the king, whereas a minister appears only on formal occasions.
